full_judgment:
34. The answer to the questions which have been debated at the Bar does, in ultimate analysis, depend upon the legal position whether the satisfaction of the detaining authority as to the necessity of making an order to detain a person, required by section 3(1) of the Special Powers Act, 1974, is purely subjective and, as such, is not justiciable at all. If the law has authorised the detaining authority to act on its own opinion, which is purely subjective, the Court cannot enquire whether there was any objective basis for such opinion. Under the English law, the writ of habeas corpus is a prerogative process for securing the liberty of a citizen by affording an effective means of his release from wrongful detention, whether in prison or in private custody. Whenever the legality of the detention is challenged in a court of law in an appropriate proceeding, the burden is upon the detaining authority to justify such detention to be in accordance with law and very often such authority invokes, in support of its act of detention, specific provision of a positive law providing for such detention on its being satisfied as to the existence of certain circumstances authorising such detention. When the law of the land confers a power upon a certain authority to detain a person on being satisfied as to the existence of such circumstances, the nature of such power of detention had been the subject of controversy in the Courts of law in England as well as in the Indian subcontinent. 

 36. According to the views expressed in some of the earlier cases in England, the satisfaction of the detaining authority required by an enactment authorising detention, if not qualified by any contrary expression, was a subjective one and the only thing which the Court could enquire was whether the authority concerned was "honestly satisfied", that is, whether there was any mala fide in the making of the impugned order and the burden to establish such mala fide was upon the person who alleged it. But if the law provided that the order could be made if the authority was "reasonably satisfied", it meant that there were, in fact, reasonable grounds for such satisfaction and the burden was upon the authority to establish that there were, in reality, certain grounds from which a reasonable man would be satisfied as to the necessity of making the order of detention and the order could be struck down if the Court was of opinion that there were no such grounds. 

 37. The judicial controversy as to whether the detaining authority's opinion is subjective or objective was brought into bold relief since the case of Liversidge Vs. Anderson, 1942 AC 206, where the majority view of the House of Lords was in favour of the detaining authority privilege of making a decision under a Regulation made under the Emergency Powers (Defence) Act, 1939 on its subjective satisfaction alone, which was immune from any judicial scrutiny, in spite of the requirement of the said Regulation that the detaining authority had, before making an order of detention, a “reasonable cause to believe" that such detention was necessary. Lord Atkin, however, in his dissenting speech, observed that every imprisonment without trial and conviction was prima facie unlawful and that the burden was upon the detaining authority to justify the detention by establishing the legality of the action according to the principles of English law. The majority view in the case of Liversidge Vs. Anderson had been the cause of much controversy in the Courts of law as well as, in the forensic literature both in England and in India, as it purported to brush aside the distinction between the expression 'satisfaction' and 'reasonable satisfaction’ for 'satisfaction on reasonable grounds', as had been so long recognised in the authoritative judicial pronouncement Reference may be made in this connection to the case of Shearer Vs. Shields, 1914 AC 802 where me House of Lords held, in construing a provision of the Glasgow Police Act, which authorised the constables to arrest if they had grounds of 'reasonable suspicion', that the burden rested upon the constable concerned to show that the suspicion was reasonable. 

 39. The view as to the invalidity of Rule 26 of the Defence of India Rules as expressed in the above decision was overruled by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Emperor Vs. Shibrath Banerjee, AIR 1945 PC 156 which held, relying upon sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Defence of India Act, that the general language of the said sub-section amply justified the terms of Rule 26 and that as such it did not go-beyond the rule-making power and was not invalid. In this case, the order of detention was made under Rule 26 as referred to above which required 'satisfaction' and not 'reasonable satisfaction' of the detaining authority as to the necessity of making the order, and it was held in the said case, relying upon section 16 of the Parent Act, that though the Court had jurisdiction to investigate the validity of an order made under the said Rule, but the burden of proof lay heavily on the person who challenged that it had not been made in conformity with the power conferred by the said Rule. Liversidge Vs. Anderson was not followed, but it was Shearer Vs. Shields, which was followed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Counsel in the case of Emperor Vs. Vimlabai Deshpande, AIR 1946 PC 123, and a distinction was made in the said case between Rule 26 and Rule 129 of the Defence of India Rules, as under Rule 26 the Government concerned could pass the order of detention if it was 'satisfied' that it was necessary to do so, whereas under Rule 129 a police officer could arrest a person whom he 'reasonably suspects' of having acted in a prejudicial manner. In the former case, the subjective satisfaction of the authority concerned was sufficient and as such it was not justiciable, but in the latter case the burden was upon the constable concerned to show that his suspicion as on reasonable grounds and his act was justified, and the Court could therefore investigate as to the reasonable basis of such suspicion. 

 54. An important question which arises from this proposition is whether in case one or some of the grounds, but not all, are found to be bad, being irrelevant or non-existent or vague, the Court can pronounce that the remaining grounds, which may not be found to be defective in any way, are sufficient for sustaining the order of detention. Since the Court is not competent to examine the adequacy or sufficiency of the grounds, which under the law, as it stands, is within juris-diction of the detaining authority, it is not in a position to say that the good grounds, after excluding the bad ones, are sufficient for the satisfaction of the detaining authority as to the necessity of making the order of detention. The burden having been upon the detaining authority to establish the legality of the order of detention the Court under the said circumstance cannot but declare that the detention cannot be sustained. 

 71. Generally in a habeas corpus proceeding the Court is to have regard to the legality or otherwise of the detention at the time of the return and not with reference to the date of the institution of the proceeding or the date of the commencement of the detention. It is, therefore, difficult to hold, in the absence of proof of bad faith, that the detaining authority cannot, independently of an earlier order of detention challenged as illegal make a fresh order, whenever possible which is free from defects and duly complies with the requirements of the law in this behalf. Reference may be made in support of this view, to a decision of The Federal Court of India in the case of Basanta Chandra Ghose Vs. Emperor, AIR, 1945 FC 18, and to two decisions of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Narayan Singh Nathuram Vs. State of Punjab AIR 1952 (SC) 106 and Ram Narayan Singh Vs. The State of Delhi AIR, 1953 (SC) 277. Similar view was also taken by the High Court Division in the case of Sharafuddin Ahmed Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs (1975) 27 DLR, 658. I would not, therefore, declare the detention to be bad only because the initial detention was invalid. But as I have already held that as the detention of the appellant is not sustainable in law on other grounds stated above I would allow this appeal.
